newsitem.title: POLAND: Tourists abducted in Yemen return to Poland.
newsitem.headline: Tourists abducted in Yemen return to Poland.

text.p: Five Polish tourists arrived back in Warsaw on Thursday after being held hostage by tribesmen in Yemen for eight days and said their abductors were poor people pressing the government for the most basic facilities of life.

"These very poor people wanted to be assured by the government that they will get part of the money extended as aid by Western countries," PAP news agency quoted Ewa Adamska, a member of the tourist group, as saying.
"They demand basics -- a teacher, electric light and road construction," she said.

Adamska and four other members of the Polish Explorers' Society were released on Wednesday after being held hostage by the al-Masni tribe in the Khawlan area of Yemen, about 65 km (40 miles) east of the capital, Sanaa.
The three men and two women, aged between 50 and 64, were kidnapped on their way to archaeological sites.

The Polish consul in Sanaa, Stanislaw Smolen, said earlier Yemeni authorities had assured the tribesmen they would not be prosecuted for the kidnapping or for a grenade attack on government security forces last Friday.
The Poles said they had not felt their lives were in danger their ordeal but some of the kidnappers treated them roughly.
"They did not want to harm us...On the whole we were treated well, although two or three kidnappers behaved brutally," Adamska said.
Zbigniew Hauser, the organiser of the ill-fated trip, said the group's last two days in captivity were the worst.
"They kept us in a dark cell and threatened us with guns when we wanted to go outside to wash," Hauser said.
In recent years, tribes in Yemen with grievances against the government or foreign oil firms have kidnapped tourists or other foreigners to use them as bargaining chips.
It was the second abduction of European holidaymakers in Yemen within a month. On December 19 five Dutch tourists were freed after being held briefly by tribesmen in an area north of Sanaa.
